choices.content: Yes, as long as its slope is 1
No, at least one of the two intercepts is 0
Yes, by setting both \(a\) and \(b\) to 0
No, because the origin has no coordinates

question.prompt: Can a line through the origin be written in intercept form \(x/a+y/b=1\)?

solutions.explanation: Intercept form requires both intercepts to be nonzero. For a line through the origin, at least one intercept is 0.
solutions.title: Use the intercept-form restriction

solutions.explanation: For \(x/a+y/b=1\) to be defined, \(a\ne0\) and \(b\ne0\). A line through the origin must contain \((0,0)\), but substituting these coordinates gives \(0/a+0/b=0\), whereas the equation requires the left side to equal \(1\). Thus no line through the origin has this intercept form. The answer is B.
solutions.title: Substitute the origin
